tagline.text: A seaside promenade in the city where sunsets and charcoal-grill stalls close out the day

location.label: Location
location.text: Seaside promenade, San Miguel, Puerto Princesa, Palawan (end of Rizal Avenue)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱150–600 (per person, snacks, meals and drinks)

children.text: The Puerto Princesa Baywalk is a seaside promenade about 200–300 m long along the city's waterfront. At sunset it comes alive with the evening glow, families out for a walk, and stalls grilling skewers and seafood, making it the city's signature evening spot. Entry is free, and there is almost no shade during the day.

The Puerto Princesa Baywalk is the seaside promenade in Puerto Princesa, the capital of Palawan. The city sits on Puerto Princesa Bay, and the Baywalk looks out over the calm water inside the bay. Reviews put its length at roughly

, and it is best thought of not as a big park but as a short promenade with a paved plaza and food stalls. There is no entrance fee, and OpenStreetMap places it in the Seaside area of San Miguel. Although Puerto Princesa is on Palawan, it is an independent city governed by the city rather than the province, and it is the largest city in the Mimaropa region. It faces the Sulu Sea to the east and the South China Sea to the west, and as the gateway to Palawan many travelers stay a night here before or after El Nido or Coron. The Baywalk is known as a comfortable way to spend that night.

The appeal here is all about timing. Many reviews say that during the day there is almost no shade, the sun is strong, and few stalls are open. As sunset approaches this changes, and one description says that by around 6 PM the whole strip is alive. The usual way is to walk along as the evening glow spreads over the bay and then eat skewers and seafood grilled over charcoal at the stalls. One travel guide describes it as a place that is "not a party and not pretending to be one," and it is best understood as an evening scene where families and locals come out at an easy pace rather than a loud club district. It is the simplest choice for your first night in town, the evening after an Underground River tour, or any time you want to rest by the sea close to your lodging.

The food is not expensive. One blog says a meal of pork barbecue, chicken inasal, and rice with a bottle of water comes to under ₱300, while another guide lists beer and street food at ₱15–200 and grilled squid by the seafront at about ₱100–200. Prices differ by vendor, and some reviews find them higher than the restaurants on Rizal Avenue, so it is safest to ask the price before ordering. Advice from visitors is that stalls with the longest lines of local families are usually the reliable ones. Even so, to a foreign traveler it is a much cheaper meal than a city restaurant, which makes it a good light dinner after a day of activities. Do not expect the same stalls and menu every day, though, because opening hours and menus change from day to day.

Puerto Princesa is a city that starts early, since it is the departure point for daytime plans such as the Underground River tour and Honda Bay island hopping. Tours often start between 5:00 and 6:30 AM, so the realistic plan is a light meal at the Baywalk in the evening and an early night rather than a late one. Local news reports that a night market ran at the Baywalk from April 10 to 24, 2026, and that the city tourism office said it was discussing making it permanent with the organizer. Whether it has been confirmed as a permanent fixture, and on which regular dates it runs, is not confirmed, so check locally before you go.
Walk along the bay and watch the sun go down. It is hot with no shade during the day, but the breeze cools down from late afternoon. The hour before sunset is the best time for photos.
After dark the stalls light charcoal braziers and grill pork barbecue, chicken inasal, squid, shrimp, and more. Prices can be similar to or higher than regular restaurants, so ask before you choose.
Local families come out with their children to walk and sit. Some descriptions mention a playground, bicycle rentals, and exercise space, but these may vary over time.
Reviews mention acoustic music, band performances, and decorative events. There is no known fixed schedule, so think of it as a pleasant surprise if you catch one.

Nearby on Rizal Avenue are restaurants such as Kinabuchs Grill & Bar (348 Rizal Avenue) and Kalui Restaurant (369 Rizal Avenue). Kinabuchs is known for local dishes such as tamilok and crocodile, and Kalui for a set menu that changes daily.
With no entrance fee, it is easy to slot in between an Underground River trip and a hopping tour. The atmosphere after the lights come on is completely different from daytime.

blocks.title: Easy to connect to the rest of your evening

children.text: After eating at the Baywalk it is easy to walk to a bar on Rizal Avenue or go back to your lodging, so it fits into a short evening plan. Some places stay open late, so on nights when you do not need to sleep early you can have one more drink.
Take a tricycle from your lodging to the Baywalk. This is when the daytime heat starts to ease.
Walk along the promenade and watch the sunset.
When all the stalls are open, pick skewers and grilled food from a stall with a long line.
Walk among the stalls and try one or two things such as grilled squid or skewers. It is better to order a little at a time than a lot at once.
Move to Rizal Avenue for a proper dinner or a beer at a restaurant.
Return to your lodging early and get ready for the next day's tour.
On days when a tour leaves early, set a time so that you do not stay out late.

Sunset times change with the season, so check a sunset-time app and arrive about 30 minutes early to get the best spot. On weekends many local families come out and the lines at the stalls get longer, so allow extra time.

Lodging is concentrated along Rizal Avenue and the city center, so it is convenient to choose a place within easy walking distance of the Baywalk. Hotel names and rates vary a lot by season, so check on a booking site. The city center mixes hotels and hostels at different prices so you can choose by budget, and it helps to search by distance, with a short tricycle ride to the Baywalk as the guide. Because tours start early, ask in advance whether your lodging can prepare breakfast or a packed meal. Book early in peak season.

Besides the Baywalk stalls, Rizal Avenue has Kinabuchs Grill & Bar. It is known as a big place with a garden of more than 200 seats, pool tables, and sports screens, and its menu includes tamilok, crocodile sisig, and grilled pork belly. Kalui offers a set menu that changes daily; it is best to reserve dinner one or two days ahead, and guides say it is closed on Sundays. For breakfast, a bakery selling ensaymada, pandesal, and suman is known. At the Baywalk stalls you choose skewers and seafood grilled over charcoal on the spot, so if you dislike fishy smells and smoke, sit upwind. Ask about freshness and how a seafood item is cooked if it is your first time, and choose fully cooked food if you are worried about an upset stomach.
Go before sunset, watch the sky, and eat when the stalls open.
Stalls with long lines are generally the reliable ones.
Ask the price before you order. It differs by vendor.
Many places do not take cards, so bring cash.
There is no shade during the day, so bring a hat and sunscreen.
Tours leave early, so do not stay out late.
Bring mosquito repellent to make the evening stroll more comfortable.
If you stay a day around your trip to El Nido or Coron, an evening at the Baywalk fits well into your plan.
Guides say Underground River permits for November–May should be booked 2–6 months ahead, so check early in your trip planning.
Buying a local beer and a snack and watching the sunset from a bench on the promenade is a satisfying evening on its own.
Whether the night market runs regularly and each stall's hours are not fixed, so check locally before you go.
